nodes.description: Akkermansia muciniphila is a mucin-degrading symbiont of the colonic mucus layer that uses host-derived mucus as its primary carbon and nitrogen source, placing it directly at the host-microbe interface. Its relative abundance is reduced in obesity, type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome and correlates inversely with body weight in rodents and humans. Loss of this population removes a signal that supports mucus-layer thickness and epithelial barrier integrity, and is the state that A. muciniphila-directed interventions are designed to compensate for.

nodes.description: The share of ingested energy that is absorbed rather than excreted in feces is a determinant of energy balance that sits upstream of adipose expansion. In diet-induced obese mice, pasteurized A. muciniphila lowers food energy efficiency and raises fecal energy excretion, apparently through reduced carbohydrate absorption and faster intestinal epithelial turnover, implying that the untreated state retains a correspondingly larger fraction of ingested energy.

evidence.reference_title: The role of leptin and ghrelin in the regulation of food intake and body weight in humans: a review.
evidence.snippet: In obese subjects the circulating level of the anorexigenic hormone leptin is increased, whereas surprisingly, the level of the orexigenic hormone ghrelin is decreased. It is now established that obese patients are leptin-resistant.

nodes.description: Thinning of the colonic mucus layer and loss of epithelial barrier integrity allow bacterial lipopolysaccharide to reach the systemic circulation, producing the low-grade endotoxemia that couples the gut to adipose inflammation and insulin resistance. A. muciniphila supports barrier function at least partly through its abundant outer-membrane protein Amuc_1100, a Toll-like receptor 2 ligand that survives pasteurization.

nodes.description: Daily oral capsules of pasteurized Akkermansia muciniphila MucT (heat-treated 30 minutes at 70 C; 3 x 10^10 inactivated cells per capsule) taken during the weight maintenance phase that follows a low-energy diet. Heat inactivation removes the oxygen sensitivity and manufacturing constraints of the live organism while preserving the thermostable outer-membrane protein Amuc_1100, and in rodents it increased rather than abolished the metabolic benefit. The indication tested is maintenance of weight already lost, not weight loss itself.

nodes.description: After energy restriction the body defends its previous mass through a coordinated set of responses: resting energy expenditure falls disproportionately to fat-free mass, anorexigenic signals fall while orexigenic signals rise, and shrinking adipocytes generate extracellular-matrix stress and immune activation in subcutaneous adipose tissue. Adipose tissue additionally retains a transcriptional and epigenetic memory of the prior obese state that primes it for accelerated regain. This node, rather than weight loss itself, is what maintenance therapy targets.

evidence.reference_title: Mechanisms of weight regain after weight loss - the role of adipose tissue.
evidence.snippet: we show that weight loss-induced variations in cellular stress, extracellular matrix remodelling, inflammatory responses, adipokine secretion and lipolysis seem to be associated with the amount of weight that is regained after successful weight loss

evidence.reference_title: Adipose tissue retains an epigenetic memory of obesity after weight loss.
evidence.snippet: Mice carrying this obesogenic memory show accelerated rebound weight gain
